title: Hold one heading. Where do you end?
hook: Point your ship a little north of east and never turn. Do you ever arrive?

knows: compass headings in degrees from north
that the equator is about 10,000 km from the pole
doesNotKnow: that a constant heading spirals into the pole
that the spiral has endless turns but a finite length

misconception: Holding a constant compass heading takes you around the world and back, or never anywhere in particular.
objective: The learner can say that a constant heading of 80° from the equator spirals into the North Pole after about 57,600 km (the 10,008 km north distance divided by cos 80°), circling it endlessly but over a finite length.
keyState: Heading 80° chosen (length and turns readouts at 57,630 km and 6.4) and the view zoomed on the pole to see the turns tighten.

claims.text: Holding a heading of 80° from the equator, you reach the North Pole after about 57,630 km.
claims.source: Loxodrome arc length s = R Δφ / cos α, α measured from the meridian (Snyder 1987, ch. 7; Bowditch, American Practical Navigator; from memory). 6,371.0088 × (π/2) / cos 80° = 57,631 km. Demo.tsx lengthKm, the value the readout shows. Matches the cm-geography brief. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: 6371.0088 x pi/2 / cos 80 deg = 57,631 km, shown as 57,630.

claims.text: At 80° the path circles the pole about 6.4 times by 89.9°N.
claims.source: Longitude travelled λ = tan α · ψ(φ), ψ = ln tan(45° + φ/2). tan 80° × ψ(89.9°) / 2π = 5.671 × 7.044 / 6.283 = 6.36 turns (builder node run; Demo.tsx turnsBy). Brief: 6.4. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: tan 80 x ln tan(45+89.9/2) / 2pi = 6.358, shown as 6.4.

claims.text: Closer to the pole the path keeps circling without end, but its length is finite.
claims.source: ψ(φ) → ∞ as φ → 90°, so λ → ∞ (infinitely many turns), while s = R Δφ / cos α stays finite (Snyder 1987, ch. 7; from memory). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

claims.text: Straight north from the equator to the pole is about 10,010 km.
claims.source: R · π/2 = 10,007.6 km on the sphere R = 6,371.0088 km; shown as 10,010 km (rounded to 10 km). The question's option says 'about 10,000 km'. On the WGS84 ellipsoid the meridian quadrant is 10,001.97 km (from memory). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Node: 10,007.6 km, shown as 10,010.

claims.text: Every kilometre along a constant heading gains the same amount of northing, so the length is the north distance divided by cos(heading).
claims.source: dφ/ds = cos α / R for a constant azimuth α; integrate from 0 to π/2. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

claims.text: A constant heading is called a rhumb line; it is straight on a Mercator map and a spiral on the globe.
claims.source: Snyder (1987), Map Projections: A Working Manual, USGS PP 1395, ch. 7: rhumb lines (loxodromes) are straight on the Mercator; on the sphere they spiral toward the poles (from memory). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 6): Re-derived; no issue.

recall.question: A ship keeps exactly the same compass heading, a little north of east, forever. What happens?
options: It goes round the world and returns to its start
It spirals into the North Pole after a finite distance
It wanders forever and never gets anywhere
recall.why: Each kilometre gains the same northing (cos of the heading), so it reaches the pole after the north distance divided by cos(heading), circling ever tighter on the way.
